slice: Differential diagnosis and test method for motocross / cross-country suspension (2020-2027 KTM, Husqvarna, GasGas, Yamaha, Honda, Kawasaki, Triumph TF). Drawn from tuners, testers, magazines and forums, not bike makers' manuals. Researched 2026-10-15. All text is paraphrased. Numbers appear only where a source stated them. Terminology note: when Keefer and MXA say 'sag too high' they mean the rear rides high (a smaller sag figure), and 'sag too low' means the rear rides low (a larger sag figure). The app should always speak in ride-height terms to avoid confusion.

symptoms.where: Corner entry to mid-corner (Keefer's area 2), flat or slick turns, and on the gas at the exit

causes.cause: Rear riding too low (soft shock HSC, or too much sag), which takes weight off the front
tells: Pushes on the gas or when driving through the turn
Rear feels low or squats out of corners
Bike feels stable on straights but lazy to turn
causes.first_change: Stiffen shock high-speed compression slightly. If that is not enough, take a little sag out (more preload).
causes.why: HSC holds the rear up under load, putting weight back on the front. Keefer usually tries HSC before sag.

causes.cause: Fork too stiff (compression or air), so it rides high and does not settle into the turn
tells: Push happens off the gas at entry (area 2)
Fork also deflects and feels harsh through the bars
causes.first_change: Soften fork compression (Keefer says two clicks for WP/KYB, one click for Showa), or lower air pressure slightly on an air fork
causes.why: A softer fork sinks into the stroke at entry, which steepens the effective steering angle and loads the tire

causes.cause: Forks set low in the clamps (dropped), which slows the steering
tells: Stable on the gas and at speed, but slow side to side
causes.first_change: Raise the forks a few mm in the clamps
causes.why: Raising the fork tubes steepens the head angle and moves weight forward

causes.cause: Fork rebound too fast, so the front rises and climbs out of ruts
tells: Front climbs out of ruts or pushes in area 2
causes.first_change: Slow fork rebound one click at a time
causes.why: Slower rebound keeps the front settled in the stroke through the turn

check_first.check: Front tire pressure and wear. If pressure is low, the sidewall rolls and the front loses grip in turns. The tell is more than about 4mm of rim clean.
check_first.why: A tire fault reads as a fork or geometry problem

check_first.check: Measure rear sag correctly before touching any clicker
check_first.why: Clickers cannot fix the wrong ride height

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Making large fork-height changes to fix push. Keefer calls more than 5-7mm of fork-height change excessive, and Race Tech says lowering the front end usually does not improve turning.

rider_words: front bites too hard then lets go
symptoms.where: Corner entry, during or just after braking, and on lean

causes.cause: Fork too soft (low air or soft compression), so it dives under braking
tells: Happens on the brakes at entry
Also bottoms or dives on braking bumps
causes.first_change: Stiffen fork compression first (or add air on an air fork). If the front still feels low, slide the forks down in the clamps a little.
causes.why: Holds the fork up in its stroke so the steering does not steepen suddenly. Keefer's stated order is compression first, then fork height.

causes.cause: Shock LSC too soft, so the rear unloads abruptly when you chop the throttle and pitches the bike nose-down
tells: Abrupt weight transfer when chopping throttle
causes.first_change: Stiffen shock low-speed compression
causes.why: Slows the pitch from rear to front on deceleration

causes.cause: Rear riding too high (too little sag or shock HSC too stiff): a front-low, rear-high stinkbug attitude
tells: Bike feels nose-down even on straights
Rear harsh or deflects on square edges
causes.first_change: Add sag (lower the rear) or soften shock HSC
causes.why: Restores the front-to-rear balance and slows the steering

causes.cause: Forks raised too far in the clamps
causes.first_change: Slide the forks down a few mm
causes.why: Slackens the steering geometry

causes.cause: Grabby front brake bite or shortened wheelbase after a gearing or axle change (forum reports, disputed)
tells: Started after a gearing or rear axle change, or happens only on hard initial brake application
causes.first_change: Return the axle to the previous position, or check the brake setup
causes.why: Forum users reported that axle position and brake bite changed tuck. They disagreed on which way weight moves.

check_first.check: Confirm the spring or air rate suits the rider's weight, and measure sag correctly
check_first.why: An under-sprung front dives no matter where the clickers are set

check_first.check: Note whether the axle position or gearing changed recently
check_first.why: MXA says the rear axle position changes how stiff the shock feels and changes the chassis

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Softening a fork that feels harsh while it dives. MXA and Ping both warn that a too-soft fork feels stiff because it rides deep in the stroke.

symptoms.where: Fast straights through bumps, on the gas out of corners, or under braking into corners

causes.cause: Loose steering head bearings
tells: Happens everywhere, not tied to one zone
With the front wheel off the ground, the bars fall to the stop on their own and bounce
causes.first_change: Adjust the head bearings (Bones: to the loosest acceptable setting; loosen the bottom clamp bolts, not the top ones, so fork height stays the same)
causes.why: Free play lets the front oscillate

causes.cause: Fork too stiff, or fork rebound too slow, with a light front on acceleration
tells: Front wheel skips over bumps, then dances
causes.first_change: Soften fork compression or speed up fork rebound
causes.why: Lets the front wheel follow the ground while it is lightly loaded

causes.cause: Fork rebound too fast
causes.first_change: Slow fork rebound
causes.why: Keefer lists headshake on the gas among the effects of rebound that is too fast. This competes with the 'too slow' cause above, so the app should test both directions.

causes.cause: Rear too low or soft, which makes the front light
causes.first_change: Raise the rear (less sag) if the fork changes do not cure it
causes.why: Puts weight back on the front

causes.cause: Rear too high, which puts too much weight on the front at speed
causes.first_change: Add sag (lower the rear)
causes.why: MXA says a high rear shifts weight forward and raises headshake risk at speed

causes.cause: Fork dives under braking into the firm part of the stroke
causes.first_change: Control dive (stiffer fork compression or support). Bones names the cause but gives no specific fix.
causes.why: The steep head angle plus firm mid-stroke valving sets off the shake

check_first.check: Steering head bearing drop test with the front wheel off the ground
check_first.why: This is the mechanical cause, and it is free to rule out

check_first.check: Ask whether it happens on the gas or on the brakes
check_first.why: The answer splits the suspension causes into separate branches

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Over-tightening the head bearings as a steering damper without first finding out whether the shake is an acceleration problem or a braking problem

symptoms.where: Braking bumps, jump faces and lips, G-outs, square edges, rocks, roots

causes.cause: Rebound too fast
tells: After a G-out, a jump face or a big compression (the big single hit)
causes.first_change: Slow rebound, two clicks at a time
causes.why: Controls how fast the stored spring energy is released

causes.cause: Compression too stiff, especially HSC
tells: On square edges, rocks and roots
causes.first_change: Soften compression (1-2 clicks first, per Keefer). Slavens says compression problems often need internal work.
causes.why: The shock cannot absorb the hit, so the bump drives the chassis up instead

causes.cause: Rebound too slow (packing)
tells: The first bump is fine, then it gets worse through a series
Rear sits lower with each hit
causes.first_change: Speed up rebound a couple of clicks
causes.why: The shock returns before the next bump

causes.cause: Compression too soft, so it blows through the stroke and bounces off the bottom
tells: Uses all its travel on the hit
causes.first_change: Add compression (MXA's rule of thumb: try more compression before more rebound)
causes.why: Keeps the shock out of the end of its stroke

causes.cause: Shock LSC too soft, or fork too soft (low front lets the rear kick on braking bumps)
tells: Kicks on braking bumps while off the throttle
causes.first_change: Stiffen shock LSC, or stiffen the fork (compression or air)
causes.why: Keefer links a low front and a soft-LSC rear to rear kick on braking bumps

check_first.check: Linkage bearing condition: notchiness, play, creaks
check_first.why: A vendor reports that worn bearings cause sideways kick over chop and square edges

check_first.check: Have a helper watch the rear wheel over a jump or whoops
check_first.why: Telling 'too fast' from 'too slow' rebound often needs an outside observer

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Always slowing rebound. MXA lists four different causes of kick, and slow rebound kicks as much as fast rebound.

rider_words: rear sits down out of corners
symptoms.where: Corner exits on the gas, rollers, acceleration bumps

causes.cause: Shock HSC too soft
causes.first_change: Turn HSC in (MXA: a quarter turn)
causes.why: HSC sets the rear ride height under load

causes.cause: Shock LSC too soft
tells: Bottoms more than 2-3 times a lap
causes.first_change: Stiffen LSC 1 click
causes.why: A flatter ride with less pitching

causes.cause: Rear riding too low (too much sag)
tells: Rear feels low even at walking speed
causes.first_change: Raise the rear slightly (less sag)
causes.why: Restores the ride height

causes.cause: Rebound too fast
tells: Moves side to side at slight lean
causes.first_change: Slow rebound
causes.why: Keefer lists diving on acceleration bumps as a symptom of rebound that is too fast

causes.cause: Long wheelbase (axle far back)
tells: Squats on acceleration and the front is light out of corners
causes.first_change: Shorten the wheelbase
causes.why: In Keefer's KTM test, a shorter swingarm length reduced squat and improved front traction out of corners

check_first.check: Late in the moto? Suspect shock oil heat fade
check_first.why: A shock holds little oil and fades badly when hot

check_first.check: Rear tire pressure. If it is too low, the bike wallows through bumps.
check_first.why: A tire fault mimics soft damping

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Adding preload to stop squat when the rear is only low under load. MXA and Keefer use HSC for ride height in motion.

symptoms.where: Straights at speed, braking zones, landings

causes.cause: Too little sag (too much preload)
tells: High rear while seated and while stopped
Harsh or deflecting rear on square edges
causes.first_change: Add sag
causes.why: Lowers the rear and rebalances the bike

causes.cause: Shock HSC too stiff
tells: Rear high once moving but sag measures correct
causes.first_change: Turn HSC out
causes.why: HSC sets the dynamic ride height

causes.cause: Fork too low (soft fork or forks raised in the clamps)
causes.first_change: Slide the forks down or stiffen the fork
causes.why: Balance depends on both ends together

causes.cause: New shock not yet broken in
tells: A brand-new or freshly serviced shock
causes.first_change: Re-check sag after break-in (MXA: about two hours)
causes.why: MXA says a new shock sits high until it is broken in

causes.cause: Hot shock
tells: Sag reads differently when hot than when cold
causes.first_change: Measure sag the same way each time; MXA suggests measuring after practice
causes.why: MXA says a hot shock can sit higher

check_first.check: Peg-press balance test (spring forks): stand on one peg off the stand and push down. Both ends should compress about equally.
check_first.why: Shows quickly which end is out of balance

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Fixing only the rear when the fork is the end that is low. MXA calls this the butterfly or seesaw effect.

symptoms.where: Corner exits, acceleration chop, hard-pack, at lean

causes.cause: Rear riding too high
causes.first_change: Soften HSC to drop the rear slightly. Keefer tries this before changing sag.
causes.why: Loads the rear tire

causes.cause: Shock LSC too stiff
causes.first_change: Soften LSC
causes.why: Lets the rear follow small bumps

causes.cause: Rebound too slow
causes.first_change: Speed up rebound
causes.why: The tire returns to the ground faster

causes.cause: Rear riding too low under load
tells: Squats, and traction fades out of corners under power
causes.first_change: Raise the rear slightly
causes.why: Keefer lists reduced traction out of corners as a symptom of a low rear

check_first.check: Rear tire pressure. Too much causes wheelspin and leaves no rim clean, and pressure rises with heat during a moto.
check_first.why: This is the most common false suspension complaint

check_first.check: Linkage bearings
check_first.why: Worn or dry bearings reduce traction and grip out of corners

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Changing sag first. Keefer tries HSC before sag for rear traction.

rider_words: gets lower and lower in whoops
harsh by the end of the bump section
symptoms.where: Series of bumps: braking bumps, acceleration chop, whoops

causes.cause: Rebound too slow for the track speed
tells: The first hits are fine, then it gets worse through the series
causes.first_change: Speed up shock rebound a couple of clicks, then do the same at the fork
causes.why: The wheel recovers before the next bump. This is Bones's stated order.

causes.cause: Compression too soft, so the wheel goes deep and takes longer to recover
tells: Also bottoms on landings, squats on the gas, dives on the brakes
causes.first_change: Add compression
causes.why: Bones: make sure compression is in a reasonable range before blaming packing

causes.cause: Compression too stiff (MXA lists this as a packing cause)
causes.first_change: Soften compression
causes.why: A different first-hit signature from rebound packing

causes.cause: Chain too tight (mechanical)
tells: Rear harsh under load with a packing sensation
causes.first_change: Set chain slack. Keefer's KTM figure is 65-68mm measured at the swingarm slider end.
causes.why: In Keefer's back-to-back test, 60mm of slack felt harsh and packed, and 66mm felt freer

check_first.check: Note the first symptom felt in the section
check_first.why: Bones uses first-hit behavior to separate too soft, too stiff and packing

check_first.check: Chain slack
check_first.why: A too-tight chain mimics packing

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Slowing rebound to stop kicking in bumps, which makes packing worse

rider_words: no matter how soft I go it's harsh

causes.cause: Too soft, so the suspension rides deep in the firm part of the damping and the stroke
tells: Feels harsher as you click softer
Travel indicator (o-ring or band) shows deep usage
causes.first_change: Add compression to raise the fork into the plusher part of the stroke
causes.why: MXA, Ping and Keefer all describe a too-soft fork that feels stiff

causes.cause: Oil height (air volume) wrong: too high gives a harsh mid-to-end stroke, too low lets it bottom
tells: Clickers do not change the deep-stroke feel
MXA says oil height has negligible effect on the first four inches of travel
causes.first_change: Change oil height in 10cc steps per leg (MXA); use bottoming as the gauge
causes.why: Oil height changes the air spring from mid-stroke on

causes.cause: Mechanical: binding from misalignment, trapped air, or a leaking cartridge seal
tells: Started after a service, crash or wheel change
causes.first_change: Bleed the fork, then realign the fork (see mechanical_mimics)
causes.why: Race Tech calls improper installation the top cause of harshness

check_first.check: Fit a travel indicator to see where in the stroke the fork lives
check_first.why: Separates 'too soft, riding deep' from 'too stiff'

check_first.check: Fork air bleed when cold; on air forks, check pressure
check_first.why: Heat-built air pressure stiffens the stroke

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Backing the compression clickers out further, which makes the fork ride deeper and feel harsher

symptoms.where: Square edges, roots, rocks, braking bumps, on and off throttle

causes.cause: Fork initial compression too stiff, or the fork over-sprung or with oil too high
tells: On the gas with the front light
causes.first_change: Check sag, then soften fork compression. If the fork has already been resprung or revalved and the problem persists, suspect the spring is too stiff.
causes.why: Keefer lists these causes and this order for fork deflection on the gas

causes.cause: Rear riding too low, so the front rides high and light
causes.first_change: Raise the rear (less sag, or more HSC)
causes.why: A lower rear unloads the front

causes.cause: Rebound too slow, or compression stiff, off the brakes
causes.first_change: Adjust fork compression or rebound
causes.why: Keefer's off-throttle table

causes.cause: Shock HSC or LSC too stiff, or rear too high
causes.first_change: Soften shock HSC or LSC, or add sag
causes.why: Keefer lists rear deflection under these settings

check_first.check: Tire pressures
check_first.why: Rocky tracks need more pressure (MXA); too much pressure costs grip

check_first.check: Linkage bearings and fork alignment
check_first.why: Both produce harsh, deflecting feedback on sharp hits

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Softening the fork when the real cause is a low rear lifting the front

rider_words: fork is hard on my hands
symptoms.where: Braking bumps, choppy straights, slap-down landings

causes.cause: Fork compression too stiff, or air too high
causes.first_change: Soften fork compression
causes.why: More fork movement lets the fork absorb the hit

causes.cause: Fork too soft, riding in the mid-stroke under braking
tells: Harsh off throttle in braking bumps
causes.first_change: Stiffen the fork as a test. If comfort improves, the fork was too soft.
causes.why: Keefer's off-throttle harshness test

causes.cause: Fork rebound too fast, so the front end is busy and the rider over-grips
causes.first_change: Slow fork rebound
causes.why: Keefer links a busy front from fast rebound to arm pump from over-gripping

causes.cause: Fork rebound too slow, so it does not return in time during braking
tells: Gets harsher through a braking-bump series
causes.first_change: Speed up fork rebound
causes.why: Keefer's off-throttle table

check_first.check: Bleed the fork air, cold, with the front wheel off the ground
check_first.why: Built-up air makes the fork harsh

check_first.check: Fork alignment and clamp bolt torque
check_first.why: Binding produces harshness

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Going softer on a fork that is already riding deep

symptoms.where: Jump landings, flat landings, G-outs, whoops

causes.cause: Compression too soft
tells: Bottoms more than once or twice a lap (Keefer accepts once or twice)
causes.first_change: Add compression, two clicks at a time, until bottoming stops (MXA shock procedure)
causes.why: Slows the stroke

causes.cause: Spring, air or fork oil volume too low (end-of-stroke support)
tells: Mid-stroke feels fine, but the end of the stroke is weak
causes.first_change: Raise fork oil height (MXA says more oil works best for bottoming), or check air pressure and spring rate
causes.why: End-stroke support comes from the air spring

causes.cause: Worn internals, leaking seals, or low oil
tells: Bottoming that gets worse over time with no setting change
causes.first_change: Service the suspension
causes.why: Slavens lists these as bottoming causes

causes.cause: Hot shock oil (fade)
tells: Late in the moto, on hot days
causes.first_change: Address heat (see conditions)
causes.why: MXA says shocks fade badly when hot

check_first.check: Count bottoming per lap; once or twice is acceptable
check_first.why: Keeps the rider from over-stiffening

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Clicking compression all the way in to fix a spring or oil-volume problem

causes.cause: Rebound too fast or too light (loose, unstable)
causes.first_change: Try stiffer or slower rebound
causes.why: Keefer's prescription for a loose feel or blowing through the stroke on jumps

causes.cause: Shock HSC too soft
tells: No hold-up in G-outs or up jump faces
causes.first_change: Add HSC
causes.why: HSC gives hold-up on big shaft-speed events

causes.cause: Rebound too slow, so the shock stays down
tells: Feels stuck down through a series of hits
causes.first_change: Speed up rebound
causes.why: Too much rebound keeps the suspension compressed for the next hit

check_first.check: Ask whether it is a single big hit (compression or HSC) or a series (rebound)
check_first.why: This separates the two competing rebound diagnoses

symptoms.common_wrong_move: Adding rebound when the shock is already staying down

symptoms.where: Rollers, waves, whoops, transitions on and off throttle

causes.cause: Compression too soft (LSC, and HSC for ride height)
causes.first_change: Turn compression in 1 click (MXA); HSC in for a low rear
causes.why: Adds support in the mid-stroke

causes.cause: Fork oil low (more air volume)
tells: Fork is soft from mid-stroke on
causes.first_change: Add fork oil
causes.why: MXA: more oil stiffens the fork from mid-stroke

causes.cause: Tire pressure too low
tells: Wallows through bumps, front grip fades, more than 4mm of rim clean
causes.first_change: Add tire pressure
causes.why: Tire sidewall flex mimics soft damping

check_first.check: Tire pressure and rim clean
check_first.why: Cheap to rule out

rider_words: fine on big hits, harsh on small

causes.cause: Low-speed compression too stiff
causes.first_change: Soften LSC (shock) or fork compression

causes.cause: Rebound too slow

causes.first_change: Speed up rebound
causes.why: Faster rebound restores early-stroke plushness

causes.cause: Seal stiction or dry or worn bearings (friction rather than damping)
tells: Notchy or sticky feel by hand
Large gap between the push and lift sag readings

causes.why: Stiction is strongest on small bumps and light loads (MXA). A vendor says worn bearings cause harshness on small bumps.

causes.cause: Air pressure buildup in the fork

check_first.why: Separates friction from damping

rider_words: rear steps out on throttle at lean
symptoms.where: On the gas, at slight lean, in acceleration bumps

causes.cause: Rear ride height wrong (too high or too low)
tells: If the rear is high, it stinkbugs while seated
If the rear is low, it is harsh out of corners
causes.first_change: Decide which by checking harshness out of corners and stinkbug feel, then adjust sag or HSC
causes.why: Keefer's on-throttle table

causes.cause: Rebound too fast
tells: Side-to-side movement on the throttle at slight lean
causes.first_change: Slow rebound
causes.why: Keefer action/reaction list

check_first.check: Measure sag

fixes.works_because: It controls how fast the spring returns after a big single hit
fixes.choose_when: It kicks straight up after a G-out, a jump face or a big compression

fixes.works_because: The shock absorbs the edge instead of transmitting it
fixes.choose_when: It kicks sideways on square edges, rocks or roots, or is harsh through the feet. Keefer tries 1-2 clicks softer compression first for bucking.

fixes.works_because: It stops the shock blowing through and rebounding off the bottom
fixes.choose_when: It also bottoms. MXA's rule of thumb is more compression before more rebound.

fixes.works_because: It stops packing in a series of bumps
fixes.choose_when: The kick builds through a bump series rather than on the first hit

fixes.works_because: It holds the rear up under load, moving weight forward
fixes.choose_when: It pushes on the gas and the rear feels low. Keefer tries this before a sag change.

fixes.works_because: It raises the static rear ride height
fixes.choose_when: The rear is low even at walking speed or when sag measures high. It also suits tight tracks (MXA: 100mm rather than 105mm).

fixes.works_because: The fork settles into the turn and loads the front tire
fixes.choose_when: It pushes off the gas at entry and the fork also feels harsh or deflects

fixes.fix: Raise the forks in the clamps a few mm
fixes.works_because: It steepens the head angle and moves weight forward
fixes.choose_when: The bike is stable but slow to steer. Keep the total change within about 5-7mm.

fixes.choose_when: Try this first (Keefer's order)

fixes.fix: Slide the forks down in the clamps
fixes.works_because: It raises the static front ride height
fixes.choose_when: The front still feels low after the compression change

fixes.works_because: It acts like a stiffer spring
fixes.choose_when: The fork also bottoms more than 2-3 times a lap, or the air pressure is below baseline

fixes.works_because: It lowers the rear dynamically
fixes.choose_when: The rear rides high. Keefer tries this before sag.

fixes.works_because: It lowers the rear statically
fixes.choose_when: The rear is high at rest or sag measures low

fixes.fix: Soften LSC or speed up rebound
fixes.works_because: The tire follows acceleration bumps
fixes.choose_when: There is wheelspin on acceleration bumps or hard-pack chop

fixes.works_because: It enlarges the footprint
fixes.choose_when: There is no rim clean, or pressure has risen with heat

fixes.choose_when: The fork dives, the travel indicator shows deep use, or it gets harsher as you click softer

fixes.works_because: It softens from mid-stroke on without changing the first part of the stroke
fixes.choose_when: Harshness is mid-to-end stroke and the fork is not bottoming

fixes.choose_when: Sag measures low, or on fast or sandy tracks

fixes.choose_when: The rear setup is correct but the bike is nose-down

fixes.works_because: It lowers the rear in motion only
fixes.choose_when: Sag is correct but the rear rides high once moving

fixes.choose_when: The fork is plush early and only bottoms at the end

fixes.choose_when: Pressure is below baseline. Check it cold.

fixes.works_because: It controls dive
fixes.choose_when: The fork is diving (several forum posters and Keefer)

fixes.works_because: The fork recovers from braking before turn-in
fixes.choose_when: A forum suggestion (theycallmeebryan) for a fork held down by slow rebound

mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Front wheel off the ground: turn the bars about halfway to one side and let go. Bars that fall and bounce off the stop are too loose; correct bearings need a small push (Bones). Keefer: tap the bars lightly; if they swing to the stops, tighten.

mechanical_mimics.fault: Misaligned fork legs or a bound axle (wrong pinch-bolt sequence, burr on the axle step)
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Harsh fork, plus bushing and coating wear. Race Tech calls this the top cause of harshness.
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Race Tech: check the axle step for burrs by sliding the reversed axle through the fork bottom; tighten the axle with the right pinch loose; spin the wheel, grab the brake or pump the fork, and confirm the fork bottom returns to the same spot each time; then tighten the pinch bolts. MXA: turn the axle (not the nut) with the 19mm Allen, then tighten the pinch bolts.

Torque to the OEM specification. Race Tech cites typical values of about 16 ft-lb top and 14 ft-lb bottom but says to verify for the model. A forum user reported that his fork action returned once over-tight clamps were corrected (anecdote).

mechanical_mimics.fault: Bent fork tube or axle after a crash
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Fork moves freely off the bike but feels stuck once clamped; harsh
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Check axle runout with a dial indicator; suspect it if one leg slid in the clamp during the crash (forum)

mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Binding or harshness; can dent the inner tube
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Use bolts of the original length

mechanical_mimics.fault: Air pressure buildup in coil-spring forks
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Fork gets harsher through the ride
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Bleed before every ride, with the forks cool and the front wheel off the ground

mechanical_mimics.fault: Air fork outer-chamber buildup or pressure drift
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Fork feels stiffer than its air setting
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Open the bleed screws on both caps until they hiss (ADB says after each ride); check main pressure with the wheel off the ground, since a partly compressed fork reads high

mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Fork stiffens late in the moto
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Check pressure cold (Keefer). One MXA reader reported a 4 psi rise during a race and set 4 psi low to compensate.

mechanical_mimics.fault: Worn, dry or notchy linkage and swingarm bearings
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Harsh on small bumps, kicks sideways over chop or square edges, loses traction, uneven rebound
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Look for play, creaks and notchy movement. In the Race Tech sag method, a gap between the lift and push readings over about 4-5mm means the linkage needs attention. Grease periodically (MXA).

mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Harsh on small bumps and under light loads
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: No formal test found. MXA's evidence was informal fleet observation.

mechanical_mimics.fault: Leaking cartridge (inner rod) seal on Showa forks
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Harsh fork (oil migrates to the outer chamber)

mechanical_mimics.fault: Worn internals, leaking seals, low oil
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Service the unit. Factory Connection recommends a full service every 40 hours.

mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Shock feels faster and softer, and fades late in the moto
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Notice whether the fault worsens as the moto goes on and on hot days; check service hours. MXA: hot oil makes damping softer, hot nitrogen makes compression firmer, and old oil loses viscosity.

mechanical_mimics.fault: Spring sag over time, or a new shock not broken in
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Sag drifts; a new shock sits high
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Re-check sag regularly; re-measure after about two hours on a new shock (MXA)

mechanical_mimics.fault: Tire pressure wrong, or rising with heat
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Too low: wallowing and front grip loss in turns. Too high: wheelspin and poor grip. Heat: less contact-patch feel.
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Set pressure before any suspension change. Read rim clean: more than about 4mm means too low, none means too high. MXA says pressure can rise up to 6 psi rear and 3 psi front over the first three laps.

mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Harsh rear with a packing sensation under acceleration
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Measure slack at the swingarm slider end. Keefer's KTM 450 SX-F figure is 65-68mm; 60mm felt harsh and packed.

mechanical_mimics.fault: Rear axle position changed (gearing or chain)
mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Axle forward makes the shock feel stiffer and changes front weight; Keefer saw noticeable chassis change at about 10mm or more from target
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Measure swingarm pivot to axle center and log it with the setup

mechanical_mimics.feels_like: Front tucks on initial brake application
mechanical_mimics.how_to_check: Single forum report: a larger floating rotor kit reduced the bite. Unverified.

test_method.claim: Record every clicker, sag, fork height, air pressure and tire pressure before changing anything. Start from stock or baseline, and compare back to stock at the end of the day.
steps: Write down the current clickers as clicks out from fully in (MXA)
Start from the manufacturer's or a known baseline (Keefer)
Log every change; MXA's crew writes setups on the fenders
At the end of the session, ride stock back to back against your final setting. MXA says this can show that a day was wasted, often by overshooting.

test_method.claim: Fix the non-clicker variables first. Clickers cannot fix the wrong sag, the wrong air pressure or the wrong spring.
steps: Tire pressure set for the terrain
Spring rate suits the rider's weight and skill; set sag
Bleed the forks cold (coil) or the outer chambers (air), and check air pressure
Check the steering head and fork alignment
Then start clicking

test_method.topic: One change at a time and step size
test_method.claim: Change one adjuster at a time (compression or rebound, not both). Sources disagree on how big a step to take (see disagreements).
steps: Keefer: 1-2 clicks per change, one adjuster only
Keefer: KYB often needs two compression clicks to feel a difference; Showa and WP respond to one; rebound usually one click at a time
Keefer: HSC about 1/6 turn on Showa and 1/4 turn on WP or KYB to feel a change
Slavens: clickers in 2-click steps; HSC in 1/4 to 1/2 turn steps
MXA 2015 and Ping: make big changes to find the direction, then fine-tune

test_method.claim: Ride a short block of laps per setting on the same lines, so impressions stay fresh and comparable.
steps: Keefer: 2-4 laps per setting
Ping: a couple of laps
Use the same line every lap, including the rough bumps you are testing
Use a jump plus whoops for compression and rebound checks (MXA)
Note where on the track each setting works or fails. The goal is consistency across the whole track, not one section (MXA).

test_method.topic: MXA shock sequence (compression, then rebound, then compression again)
test_method.claim: Set compression against bottoming first, then rebound against kicking, then re-check compression because rebound changes affect compression.
steps: Ride a jump and whoops; if it bottoms, turn compression in two clicks; repeat until it stops
Full track: harsh means compression out one click; wallowy means in one click
Have a helper watch the rear wheel over a jump or whoops at speed; if it kicks or skips, turn rebound in two clicks; test a range, because slow rebound can kick as much as fast
Re-check compression
Use HSC for ride height: rear low means in, rear high means out

test_method.topic: Measuring rider (race) sag with friction cancelled
test_method.claim: Race Tech's three-measurement method averages out linkage friction and should repeat within 1mm.
steps: L1: bike on a stand, rear wheel off the ground, measure axle to a fixed mark, vertically
Rider in full gear stands on the pegs (dirt bike), balancing on something without a helper holding the bike, without gripping with the knees and without loading the bars
L2: push the rear down about 15mm and let it rise slowly; measure
L3: lift the rear about 15mm and let it settle slowly; measure
Sag = L1 minus the average of L2 and L3
If L2 and L3 differ by more than about 4-5mm, service the linkage
Errors: measuring with the bike on the ground, measuring at an angle, bouncing

test_method.topic: Measuring race sag the MXA way, and consistency
test_method.claim: MXA bounces the bike to settle the shock and stresses measuring the same way every time. Standing or seated, and warm or cold, vary by source.
steps: Zero the sag tool from the axle to a fender point with the bike on the stand
Rider in gear in the real riding position, feet on the pegs; MXA's helper steadies the bike
Bounce to settle, then measure
MXA 2022: measure standing, the same way every time
MXA 2013: hot and cold shocks read differently, so set sag after practice when possible
Typical MXA range: 97-105mm (sag article); 100-105mm big bikes, never below 105mm for MXA, and above 110mm hurts geometry (Hinz)

test_method.topic: Static or free sag as a spring-rate check
test_method.claim: After rider sag is set, measure how far the bike sags under its own weight. Too much means the spring is too stiff; too little means it is too soft.
steps: Set rider sag first
Measure free or static sag (MXA 2013: lift the fender on level ground and measure the movement before the wheel lifts)
MXA 2013: over 35mm suggests too stiff; none suggests too soft
MXA 2015/2022: target about 30-40mm on big bikes; over 40 is too stiff and under 30 too soft
A firmer spring can feel softer at first because it needs less preload (MXA 2015)

test_method.claim: With spring forks, stand on one peg off the stand and press down; both ends should compress about equally.
steps: Off the stand, stand on one peg
Push down and watch both ends
If one end drops much more, investigate that end

test_method.claim: Fork height is the mm of fork tube above the top clamp. Both legs must match. A few mm is noticeable, and Keefer calls more than 5-7mm of change excessive.
steps: Measure the tube height above the top clamp on both legs
Start from the factory setting
Change in small steps and log it
When adjusting steering head bearings, loosen the bottom clamp bolts so fork height does not move (Bones)

test_method.claim: Check air pressure cold, with the front wheel off the ground, using a gauge. Account for gauge-hose effects and heat rise.
steps: Bike on a stand, front wheel off the ground; a compressed fork reads high (ADB)
Screw on the pump until seated, read, adjust, then unscrew quickly; slow removal leaks air (ADB)
Reattaching the pump to re-check charges the hose and reads a few psi lower (Bikerumor, mountain-bike test)
Check after the fork has cooled to ambient (Keefer)
Keefer 2025: think in bar, since about 2 psi equals one spring-rate step
Bleed the outer chambers after each ride (ADB)

test_method.topic: See where the fork is in its stroke
test_method.claim: Use a travel indicator (an elastic band or o-ring on the fork tube) to see whether a harsh fork is riding deep or high.
steps: Fit a band around the fork tube at the seal
Ride a lap
Read the maximum travel and use it with the too-soft-feels-stiff logic

test_method.topic: When to stop clicking and change springs, oil or valving
test_method.claim: No source gives a numeric threshold. The signals they give are listed in the steps.
steps: Sag cannot be reached with sensible preload, or free sag is outside the range: change the spring (MXA)
Wrong air pressure: fix the air, not the clickers (MXA)
The problem is in the mid-to-end stroke: change the fork oil height, not the clickers (MXA)
The fork was already resprung or revalved and still deflects: suspect the spring is too stiff (Keefer)
Slavens: rear compression problems usually need internal work
Tune stock settings fully before paying for a revalve; it also gives a benchmark to judge the revalve (MXA forks)
Expect drift from heat, oil wear and shim fatigue (MXA clickers)

test_method.claim: Keefer's rule of thumb for experienced riders: for about every two compression clicks, move rebound one click the opposite way. Slavens and MXA note that rebound changes also affect compression.
steps: Change compression
Consider a compensating rebound click
Re-check compression after rebound changes

test_method.claim: Classify every complaint first by on or off throttle, then by front or rear, then by first hit or series of hits, then by corner area (entry, mid, exit).
steps: Ask: on the gas or on the brakes? (Keefer, Bones)
Which end do you feel it through: bars or pegs and seat?
First hit, or does it build through a series? (Bones: note the first symptom)
Corner area 1, 2 or 3? (Keefer)
Does it get worse late in the moto or on hot days? (heat)

conditions.change: WP via Transmoto: rider sag 112-116mm; drop the forks 5mm in the clamps; WP Xplor preload +3mm; harder springs; AER +5 psi with a couple more rebound clicks; when deep bumps form mid-race, shock HSC +2, LSC +4, rebound +2. Keefer: stiffer than stock, front higher and rear lower. MXA: about 110mm sag for wide-open or sandy tracks. Slavens: stiffen rear compression several clicks and rebound 2-3.
conditions.why: Stability and hold-up in soft, deep, rolling terrain

conditions.change: Ping: stiffen compression two or three clicks. MXA tire: if mud slows the track, drop the rear to 10 psi or lower; in shallow mud with high speed, keep standard pressure. Ping says mud weight does not change sag enough to matter.
conditions.why: Keeps the suspension up in its stroke; adds tire footprint

conditions.change: Softer and faster settings (Keefer). Slavens: soften rear compression only. Red Bull: possibly less damping.
conditions.why: Bumps are closer together with square edges; the tire needs to track

conditions.change: More compression. Slavens: stiffen rear compression 2-4 clicks and leave rebound. Keefer: widely spaced large bumps may need slower rebound.
Slavens: soften rear compression several clicks and soften rebound 2-4 clicks. MXA: raise tire pressure on rocky tracks.

Fork rebound that is too fast lets the front climb out of ruts; rebound that is too slow packs and reduces front contact (Keefer). Forum posters also stressed technique (front brake drag, looking ahead).
conditions.why: The front needs to settle and stay down in the rut

conditions.change: Less sag (MXA example: 100mm instead of 105mm); fork height raised a little
More sag; forks down; stiffer, especially for faster riders

conditions.condition: Heat, long motos, late in the moto
conditions.change: Expect shock fade (hot oil softer, hot nitrogen firmer compression), air fork pressure rise (MXA example: set about 4 psi low), and tire pressure rise (MXA: up to 6 psi rear and 3 psi front in three laps; start rear at 10 psi to reach about 14). Factory Connection says oversized bladder caps help shock consistency. Check air and sag the same way each time.
conditions.why: Damping and air springs change with temperature

conditions.change: Match the spring or air rate to weight first. Keefer: stay near the factory air setting unless very light or very heavy; riders over 220 lb may add 0.5-1 psi of tire pressure. MXA: free sag shows whether the spring suits.
conditions.why: Sag and the spring decide where in the stroke the damping works

conditions.change: Faster, more confident riders need stiffer settings; slower, older or less aggressive riders softer ones. A supercross setup is too stiff for a typical outdoor track. MXA's published clicker settings are medians from mixed-skill testers.
conditions.why: Speed changes shaft velocity and the size of the hits

positions.says: Kicking comes from incorrect rebound, not compression
Four possible causes; rule of thumb is to try more compression before more rebound
Bucking is often from compression that is too stiff, so try softer compression first; kicking on jump tops is hard to diagnose, so test both faster and slower rebound
Straight-up kick means rebound too fast; sideways kick means too much compression or packing

disagreements.topic: What is a high-speed vs low-speed event

positions.says: LSC handles slow movement such as rollers and acceleration bumps; HSC handles fast hits such as G-outs and jump faces, and sets ride height
Jump faces, landings, medium bumps and rollers are low-speed shock movement; small stutter bumps drive high-speed movement
1-2 clicks, one adjuster at a time
Go big enough to feel; one click is hard to notice; fine-tune later
Make large changes to find the direction
2-3 clicks
2 clicks; HSC 1/4 to 1/2 turn
Shock first, then forks
Front first
Whichever end bothers you most

disagreements.topic: Free or static sag spring check range

positions.says: More than 35mm suggests the spring is too stiff; none suggests too soft
30-40mm on big bikes; over 40 too stiff, under 30 too soft
Uses 'static sag' to mean sag with the rider on board and 'free sag' for bike only, which conflicts with MXA's use of 'static sag' for bike-only sag
Sag above 110mm alters geometry undesirably; MXA does not go below 105mm
WP: 112-116mm for fast sandy tracks
Typical 97-105mm; a sandy, open track might run 110mm
Rider stands on the pegs, no helper holding the bike, no bouncing; average the push and lift readings
Rider in riding position with a helper steadying the bike; bounce to settle
Measure standing; bounce first; be consistent
Rider sits in riding position and bounces
Set race sag after practice when possible, because hot and cold read differently
Let the engine cool before measuring sag
Loosest acceptable setting; tighter as a steering damper is not required
Set it so the front needs a slight push to fall, using it as a mild damper
Stay within about 1 psi of factory unless very light or heavy; check cold
Work in bar; stay within about 0.2-0.4 bar of factory; about 2 psi is one spring step; check cold
Set about 4 psi below target cold so it reaches target hot, or start slightly under-sprung
Lowering the front end usually does not improve turning
Raising the fork tubes steepens the head angle and quickens turning; a few mm is noticeable
Forum poster KurtJ99: fork height makes little difference

disagreements.topic: Rear axle position and front weight

positions.says: Forum split: one poster says a shorter wheelbase moves weight forward and makes the fork feel softer; another says moving the wheel forward takes weight off the front
A shorter swingarm length improved front traction out of corners and reduced squat
Axle forward makes the shock feel stiffer; back makes it feel softer
Start the front at 14 psi on four-strokes and the rear at 12; or start the rear at 10 to reach about 14 by lap three
12-14 psi is typical
Brand- and compound-specific pressures, mostly 12-14 psi
13 or 14 psi
Fork rebound too slow (with a stiff fork) causes headshake on the gas
Fork rebound too fast causes headshake on the gas

gaps: No motocross-specific source found on checking shock nitrogen pressure or what a low charge feels like (search hits were car and mountain-bike sources).
No source found on spoke tension or wheel bearing condition as a mimic of suspension faults.
No step-by-step check for fork bushing wear (play test) from a specialist source.
No source gives a numeric threshold for when to stop clicking and revalve; only qualitative signals.
There is little on cold-weather effects (thicker oil) for motocross; heat effects are better covered.
Triumph TF and Yamaha/Honda/Kawasaki-specific air or coil fork differences were not covered beyond brand click sensitivity (Showa vs WP/KYB).

Terminology risk: 'static sag' means rider sag at Race Tech but bike-only sag at MXA. 'Sag too high/low' in Keefer and MXA refers to rear ride height, not the mm number. The app should normalize terms.
Linkage-bearing symptom claims come from a bearing vendor (Factory Links), which has a commercial interest. The Transmoto linkage diagnosis article body was not accessible.
src-pulpmx-mechanics-2024 duplicates Keefer's framework; do not count it as independent agreement.

Several Keefer tables (on/off throttle and action/reaction) dominate the symptom mapping. More independent tuner sources (Enzo, GPR, Stillwell, Factory Connection technical staff, Race Tech book) would strengthen it.
Mud setup is thin: only Ping's compression advice and MXA's tire pressures.

Bones Bacon's MXA video lesson (This Week in MXA ep. 47) was not transcribed; the page has no text content.
Transmoto 'How-To: Diagnose & Grease Linkage Bearings' full text not retrieved (intro only).

The WP suspension troubleshooting guide referenced on ukgser (adventure-bike context) was not read.
